seeing is believing phrase

also one eyewitness is worth ten hearsays, I’ll believe it when I see it

classical

Plaut. Truc. 489: plūris est oculātus testis ūnus quam aurītī decem

Plūris est oculātus testis ūnus quam aurītī decem.

one witness with eyes is worth more than ten with ears

(vōx cōmica: Plaut.)

The soldier’s maxim in the Truculentus; he goes on: those who hear tell what they have heard, those who see know for certain.

Other words

  • Vidē et crēde.

    also used · modern · Traupman 258

    Traupman’s phrase, literally “see and believe”. We have found no ancient source for it in Lewis & Short or the loci collections.

Examples

  • plūris est oculātus testis ūnus quam aurītī decem; quī audiunt audīta dīcunt, quī vident plānē sciunt

    one eyewitness is worth more than ten who have only heard; those who hear tell what they heard, those who see know for certainPlaut. Truc. 489–490

SourcesJohn C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency.

Plautus, Truculentus 489–490.
